title: You Can't Opt Out of Preparing Students for the World They're Entering
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Andrew Marcinek, a district edtech leader with 23 years in education, responds to no-screens-in-school and device opt-out groups that circulate parent screenshots of inappropriate content on school Chromebooks. He grants that filter breaches are real but argues that collecting worst-case examples is not data, and that routine filter gaps are ordinary IT maintenance rather than proof of systemic negligence. He points to constrained budgets, understaffed IT teams, and E-rate funding threats as context critics ignore, and cites polling in which 75 percent of parents see classroom device use as well calibrated. He concedes the case against early elementary devices and praises Seattle and Canon-McMillan for pulling back. His central analogy is graduated driver licensing: schools should phase in access with instruction, supervision and revocable privileges, including for AI, rather than ban devices outright. He closes with advice for families to report problems to district tech staff and for administrators to communicate their strategy openly.
points: Marcinek argues that cherry-picked screenshots confirm an incident occurred but say nothing about frequency, and that filter gaps are routine IT maintenance, not systemic negligence.
Districts face shrinking relief funds, aging device fleets, thin IT staffing, and an E-rate program under scrutiny partly because of screen-time anxiety.
He agrees kindergartners do not need tablets and points to Seattle and Canon-McMillan as examples of deliberate, low-friction rollbacks in the early grades.
The graduated driver licensing analogy frames device and AI access as phased, supervised and revocable, so a failure leads to recalibration rather than abolition.
School leaders should communicate openly about reductions and unresolved problems, since silence leaves a vacuum that online alarmism fills.
quotes: You cannot simply opt children out of the modern digital landscape. Your choice is either to guide them through it thoughtfully or abandon them to navigate it alone late at night without any guidance.
A tipped-off complaint box isn’t rigorous data. It confirms an issue occurred, sure, but it reveals nothing about overall frequency, regional context, or ongoing progress.
Filters act like fences, and curious students test boundaries.
A kid finds a gore site through a filter gap: that’s a crash. The response is to fix the gap, ask whether that kid should have had that device yet, and keep going.
Nobody confuses a driver’s test with being pro-car. It’s what adults do when they’ve accepted that a kid is going to drive eventually and would rather be in the car when it starts.
Every student I know is going to use these tools whether a school decides to teach them or not. The only open question is whether an adult is in the car for the first thousand miles.
When parental communication regarding technology consists solely of an annual acceptable-use contract each autumn, external critics inevitably dominate the narrative.
Refusing classroom hardware never removes a child from the digital environment
